history.s: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
history.e: The Great Pyramid was finished around 2560 BC and Cleopatra died in 30 BC, about 2,500 years later. The Moon landing came about 2,000 years after her death.

history.s: The University of Oxford is older than the Aztec Empire.
history.e: Teaching at Oxford existed by 1096. The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325.
Napoleon was about 1.70 m, roughly average for a Frenchman of his time. The myth came partly from confusion between French and British inches, and from British cartoons.

history.s: Vikings wore horned helmets in battle.
history.e: There is no evidence of this. The horned-helmet image was popularised in the 19th century, notably by costumes for Wagner's operas.

history.s: The Ottoman Empire lasted for more than 600 years.
history.e: It was founded around 1299 and dissolved in 1922. At its height it stretched across south-eastern Europe, western Asia and North Africa.

history.s: Nalanda, in present-day India, was a great centre of learning for around 700 years, attracting students from across Asia.
history.e: Nalanda flourished from about the 5th century until around 1200 AD. Its ruins are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.s: The Inca Empire kept records using knotted cords called quipu.
history.e: Quipus recorded numbers, such as taxes and census data, through the type and position of knots. Whether they also recorded language is still debated.

history.s: In the Middle Ages, most educated Europeans believed the Earth was flat.
history.e: Scholars had known the Earth was round since ancient Greece, and medieval scholars agreed. The myth spread mostly in the 19th century.

history.s: Mansa Musa, a 14th-century ruler of the Mali Empire, is often described as one of the richest people in history.
history.e: On his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, he reportedly gave away so much gold in Cairo that its value there fell for years.

history.s: The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed most of the medieval city, but very few deaths were recorded.
history.e: It burned about 13,200 houses and St Paul's Cathedral, yet only a handful of deaths were recorded. The true number is unknown.

history.s: The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and Germany was reunified in 1990.
history.e: The wall opened on 9 November 1989 and reunification followed on 3 October 1990, now Germany's national day.

history.s: Some Roman concrete structures, like the Pantheon's dome, have survived for around 2,000 years.
history.e: The Pantheon's unreinforced concrete dome is still the largest of its kind. Roman concrete may partly heal its own cracks.

history.s: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built by enslaved people.
history.e: Evidence from workers' villages and tombs shows that it was built by paid labourers and skilled craftsmen, likely including seasonal workers.

history.s: Cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation had planned streets and drainage systems over 4,000 years ago.
history.e: Cities like Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had grid layouts, brick houses, covered drains and public baths. Their script is still undeciphered.

history.s: A Japanese construction company, Kongō Gumi, operated for over 1,400 years.
history.e: It was founded in 578 AD to build a Buddhist temple and was run by the same family for centuries before becoming part of another company in 2006.

wars.s: The shortest war in recorded history lasted less than an hour.
wars.e: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 ended after about 38 to 45 minutes of British naval bombardment.

wars.s: The Hundred Years' War lasted exactly 100 years.
wars.e: The series of conflicts between England and France lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453, with long periods of truce.

wars.s: A Japanese soldier kept fighting in the Philippine jungle until 1974, because he didn't believe World War II had ended.
wars.e: Hiroo Onoda surrendered only when his former commanding officer flew out to formally relieve him of duty.

wars.s: In 1932, Australian soldiers with machine guns fought a 'war' against emus, and largely lost.
wars.e: The 'Great Emu War' tried to cull emus damaging crops in Western Australia. The fast, scattered birds proved very hard to hit.

wars.s: During Christmas 1914, some British and German soldiers stopped fighting and met in no man's land.
wars.e: In the unofficial Christmas truce, soldiers exchanged greetings, food and souvenirs, and some even played football.
World War I ran from 1914 to 1918. It began after Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria was assassinated in Sarajevo.

wars.s: At Thermopylae in 480 BC, a small Greek force including 300 Spartans held off a huge Persian army for three days.
wars.e: King Leonidas and his men were eventually outflanked, but the stand became one of history's most famous last stands.

wars.s: At the Battle of Saragarhi in 1897, 21 Sikh soldiers defended their post against thousands of attackers.
wars.e: The soldiers of the 36th Sikhs fought to the last man. 12 September is commemorated as Saragarhi Day.

wars.s: The bloodshed of the Kalinga War led Emperor Ashoka to turn to Buddhism and non-violence.
wars.e: Ashoka's remorse after conquering Kalinga (c. 261 BC) is recorded in his rock edicts. He then spread Buddhist ideas across Asia.

wars.s: The Cold War was a direct full-scale war between the United States and the Soviet Union.
wars.e: The two superpowers never fought each other directly. They competed through an arms race, the space race and proxy wars in other countries.

wars.s: In the 'Pig War' of 1859 between the USA and Britain, the only casualty was a pig.
wars.e: A border dispute over the San Juan Islands escalated after an American farmer shot a British-owned pig. The standoff ended peacefully.

wars.s: China's 19th-century Taiping Rebellion was one of the deadliest conflicts in human history.
wars.e: Estimates of the dead range from about 20 to 30 million, more than in World War I.

wars.s: Paraguay lost a large share of its population in the War of the Triple Alliance (1864–1870).
wars.e: Fighting Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay at once, Paraguay may have lost between a quarter and over half of its people, including most adult men.

wars.s: The Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history.
wars.e: Founded by Genghis Khan in 1206, at its height it stretched from Korea to Eastern Europe.

inventions.s: One of the first webcams was set up to watch a coffee pot.
inventions.e: In 1991, researchers at the University of Cambridge set up a camera so they could check the Trojan Room coffee pot without walking to it. It went online in 1993.

inventions.s: Bubble wrap was originally invented as wallpaper.
inventions.e: In 1957, two engineers tried to make textured plastic wallpaper. It flopped, but the material later found its use as packaging.

inventions.s: Thomas Edison invented the first electric light bulb.
inventions.e: Many inventors made incandescent lamps before Edison. His team's achievement was a practical, long-lasting bulb and a power system to run it.

inventions.s: Paper, printing, gunpowder and the compass were all invented in China.
inventions.e: Known as the Four Great Inventions, they transformed communication, warfare and navigation around the world.

inventions.s: In 1947, engineers found a real moth in a computer and recorded it as the 'first actual case of bug being found'.
inventions.e: The moth was taped into the Harvard Mark II logbook. The word 'bug' for a technical fault is older, but this is its most famous example.

inventions.s: The Wright brothers' first powered flight in 1903 lasted about 12 seconds.
inventions.e: Orville Wright flew 37 m (120 ft) at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Their longest flight that day lasted 59 seconds.

inventions.s: Velcro was inspired by burrs that stuck to a dog's fur.
inventions.e: Swiss engineer George de Mestral studied burrs under a microscope after a walk with his dog and saw tiny hooks. Velcro was patented in the 1950s.

inventions.s: The Internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing.
inventions.e: The Internet is the global network of computers. The Web, invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989, is one service that runs on it, like email.

inventions.s: The QR code was invented in Japan to track car parts.
inventions.e: Denso Wave, part of the Toyota group, created the QR code in 1994. It can be read quickly from any angle.

inventions.s: Kenya was a world pioneer of mobile-phone money with M-Pesa, launched in 2007.
inventions.e: M-Pesa let people send and store money by text message, without a bank account. It spread across Africa and beyond.

inventions.s: The microwave oven was invented after a radar engineer noticed a chocolate bar melting in his pocket.
inventions.e: Percy Spencer of Raytheon noticed the effect while working near a magnetron in the 1940s. Early microwave ovens were taller than a person.

inventions.s: The @ sign was chosen for email addresses in 1971.
inventions.e: Ray Tomlinson picked @ for the first networked email system because it meant 'at' and wasn't used in names.

inventions.s: The QWERTY keyboard layout was designed for typewriters in the 1870s.
inventions.e: Christopher Latham Sholes developed it for early typewriters. It stuck around long after the machines it was built for disappeared.

money.s: Paper money was first widely used in China.
money.e: Paper money called jiaozi was issued during the Song dynasty, over 1,000 years ago. Europe adopted banknotes centuries later.

money.s: On the island of Yap, giant stone discs were used as money.
money.e: Some rai stones are several metres wide. Ownership could change without moving the stone, because everyone remembered who owned it.

money.s: During Zimbabwe's hyperinflation in 2008, prices roughly doubled every day.
money.e: Inflation peaked at about 79.6 billion percent per month. Zimbabwe printed a 100 trillion dollar note.

money.s: Most modern currencies are backed by gold.
money.e: Today's currencies are 'fiat money': their value comes from government decree and public trust, not gold. The US dollar left the gold standard in 1971.

money.s: The word 'salary' is linked to the Latin word for salt.
money.e: It comes from the Latin 'salarium', related to 'sal' (salt). The popular story that Roman soldiers were paid in salt is disputed.

money.s: The worst hyperinflation ever recorded was in Hungary in 1946, when prices doubled about every 15 hours.
money.e: The pengő became so worthless that Hungary printed a 100 quintillion (10²⁰) pengő banknote.

money.s: The Dutch 'Tulip mania' of the 1630s is often cited as one of the first recorded speculative bubbles.
money.e: Rare tulip bulbs reportedly sold for more than a house before prices suddenly collapsed in 1637. Historians debate how widespread the damage was.

money.s: Every country in the European Union uses the euro.
money.e: 20 of the 27 EU countries use the euro. Others, such as Sweden, Poland and Denmark, keep their own currencies.

money.s: India's UPI system handles billions of digital payments every month.
money.e: The Unified Payments Interface lets people pay instantly by phone. Even small street vendors accept it with a QR code.

money.s: Sweden is one of the world's most cashless societies.
money.e: Cash is used in only a small fraction of payments in Sweden. Many shops and even some banks don't handle cash at all.

money.s: The first general-purpose charge card, Diners Club, appeared in 1950.
money.e: According to legend, it was inspired by a businessman who forgot his wallet at a restaurant.

work.s: Before alarm clocks were common, people called 'knocker-uppers' were paid to wake workers by tapping on their windows.
work.e: They used long poles or pea-shooters to reach upper windows. The job lasted in some British towns until the 1970s.

work.s: 'Computer' used to be a job title for people who did calculations by hand.
work.e: Human computers, often women, calculated everything from astronomy tables to rocket trajectories, including at NASA in the 1950s and 60s.

work.s: Almost all lighthouses today are automated, so the job of lighthouse keeper has nearly disappeared.
work.e: Keepers once lived at remote lighthouses to keep the lamps lit. Automation replaced most of them during the 20th century.

work.s: Mumbai's dabbawalas deliver well over 100,000 home-cooked lunches every working day.
work.e: Using bicycles, trains and a colour-coded system of marks, they deliver with remarkable accuracy and carry the empty boxes home again.

work.s: Most doctors today recite the ancient Hippocratic Oath word for word.
work.e: The original oath swears by Greek gods. Medical schools today use modern versions, such as the Declaration of Geneva, if they use an oath at all.

work.s: Professional mourners, people paid to weep at funerals, have existed in many cultures.
work.e: Professional mourning is recorded in ancient Egypt, ancient Rome and the Bible, and is still practised in parts of China and elsewhere.

work.s: Most US air traffic controllers face a mandatory retirement age of 56.
work.e: The rule reflects how demanding and high-stakes the job is. Controllers must also start training before about age 31.

work.s: Iceland trialled shorter working weeks for public workers from 2015 to 2019, with wellbeing improving and productivity maintained.
work.e: After the trials, most of Iceland's workforce gained the right to negotiate shorter hours.

work.s: Only a few hundred people have ever passed the Master Sommelier exam for wine experts.
work.e: The exam includes identifying wines by taste alone, without seeing the bottle. Many candidates attempt it several times.

work.s: Organised firefighting services began only in the 20th century.
work.e: Ancient Rome created the Vigiles in 6 AD: thousands of men who fought fires and patrolled the streets at night.

work.s: Many airlines have the pilot and co-pilot eat different meals.
work.e: If one meal causes food poisoning, the other pilot should still be fit to fly the plane.

work.s: Before refrigerators, cutting and shipping ice from frozen lakes was a major global industry.
work.e: In the 19th century, ice from New England and Norway was shipped as far as India and the Caribbean.
